analysis.one_liner: Speeds up federal environmental reviews of natural gas pipelines by putting a single agency in charge.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced: referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Energy Subcommittee in February 2023, it received no further action before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission the only lead agency for the environmental review of natural gas pipeline projects, and required every other federal, state, and local agency involved to defer to FERC's plan for that review [S2]. It set deadlines — other agencies would generally have 90 days after FERC finishes its review to issue their own approvals — and required agencies to run their reviews at the same time rather than one after another [S2][S3]. It also directed FERC to consult the Transportation Security Administration on pipeline security and cybersecurity [S2][S3]. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and a subcommittee and never received a hearing or vote [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Natural gas pipeline developers and the broader gas industry benefit most: the bill centralizes environmental review under FERC, forces other agencies to defer to FERC's review scope and deadlines, requires them to run their reviews at the same time, and lets applicants fund third-party contractors to help review their own applications — all of which shortens the time and uncertainty between filing and construction approval [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gas pipeline developers and the gas industry

how_it_helps.text: It would make FERC the sole lead agency for the NEPA environmental review of gas pipeline applications and require other agencies to defer to FERC's approved review scope [S2][S3].

It sets a deadline of no more than 90 days after FERC completes its environmental review for other agencies to issue their federal authorizations, and requires agencies to run their reviews concurrently with FERC's [S3].

It lets applicants fund third-party contractors to help review their own applications and requires agencies to accept remotely gathered (aerial) survey data, which speeds up the applicant's paperwork [S3].
It requires FERC to consult with the Transportation Security Administration on pipeline security and cybersecurity, and to publish permitting schedules and timelines on a public website [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Communities near proposed pipeline routes and anyone who relies on state, local, or tribal input into environmental review bear the cost: agencies lose the ability to demand supplemental review, comments from non-participating agencies cannot even enter the record, and environmental agencies must finish within FERC's timetable [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities near pipelines and environmental agencies

drawbacks.text: The bill requires every other federal and state agency to defer to FERC's chosen scope for the environmental review and to meet FERC's schedule, which critics of permit-streamlining measures say weakens environmental review of pipelines that cross communities and waterways [S2][S3].

An agency that misses its deadline must report the failure to Congress within 5 days and produce an implementation plan, pressuring agencies to approve on schedule even when their analysis is incomplete [S3].

Agencies would have to accept remotely gathered (aerial) survey data from applicants and could grant conditional approvals before verifying it on-site, an allowance requested by and benefiting the applicant [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill died before any hearing or vote, so its costs and benefits never got tested. Had it passed, it would have sped gas pipeline permitting and made review timelines more predictable — things the industry values and that pipeline builders would cite as lowering project costs — while shifting more of the environmental analysis under a single agency with hard deadlines and limiting the role of other agencies and the public input that comes with them. With zero cosponsors [S4] and no committee action [S1], its provisions never faced the scrutiny that would show whether those tradeoffs were well designed.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and a subcommittee in February 2023 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Burgess (R-TX) introduced the bill on February 6, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S1][S5].
On February 17, 2023, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy, Climate and Grid Security — the last action ever taken on the bill [S5].
No further action, hearing, markup, or floor vote occurred before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill died in committee [S1][S5].
The bill attracted zero cosponsors during its two years in the chamber [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Opponents of streamlined pipeline permitting — environmental agencies and groups that rely on independent environmental review of gas pipelines — are better off, since the bill never advanced; pipeline developers keep the existing, slower permitting process.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Opponents of streamlined gas pipeline permitting

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never took the bill up after the subcommittee referral — no hearing, markup, or vote was scheduled during the 118th Congress [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors of either party [S4], and died without any vote, so no partisan divisions were ever recorded.

industries.industry: Natural gas pipeline developers and operators
industries.note: The bill speeds and centralizes the permitting of interstate natural gas pipelines, shortening the time between application and construction and capping post-review authorization deadlines at 90 days. Faster approvals mean earlier revenue for pipeline companies [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Federal and state environmental and resource agencies
industries.note: Agencies other than FERC would lose their independent role in environmental review, forced to defer to FERC's scope and finish their own reviews within FERC's schedule, with public reporting to Congress if they miss deadlines. This narrows the checks these agencies can apply to pipeline projects [S2][S3].

industries.industry: Consulting firms doing pipeline permitting work
industries.note: The bill explicitly allows applicants to fund third-party contractors to help review their own applications, creating a paid role for outside consultants in the government's own review process [S3].
